Deut.25.1.note: Judicial causatives: French impersonal subjects are syntactic support, not lexical equivalents. Innocent/guilty opposition retained.

Deut.25.2.note: The idiom son of beating means deserving punishment; the number of blows and ground are supplied by French syntax/context.

Deut.25.3.note: Forty is the limit; additional beating and humiliation are separately represented. The second beating noun is contextually absorbed by the verb, not a second explicit French noun.

Deut.26.1.note: Temporal subordination repeated in French for a Hebrew connective; inheritance and possession remain distinct.

Deut.26.2.note: Hebrew source preposition from the land becomes a French locative in this construction; do not make a direct lexical equation.

Deut.26.3.note: The suffix on unto him belongs to lui, not déclare; the priest in office is an idiomatic compression of the relative clause and time expression.

Deut.27.1.note: Command, elders, people and singular commandment rendered collectively as plural; speech-introduction formula contextually absorbed.

Deut.27.2.note: Entering is supplied by French; directional preposition corresponds to dans, not an original verb entrer. Day formula is compressed into lorsque.

Deut.27.3.note: The Jordan is inferred from the preceding verse, not lexically present here; preserve contextual rather than lexical link.

Deut.28.1.note: Emphatic hearing infinitive plus verb are rendered together as obeying; high status rendered as superiority; personal suffixes and divine names correctly distinguished.

Deut.28.2.note: The demonstrative these is absorbed into the presentative voici; it is not a direct lexical equivalent.

Deut.28.3.note: Blessing formula repeats in city and field; singular field to French plural champs is not a missing lexical relation.

Deut.29.1.note: First-person speaker and audience preserved; conjunction before servants is omitted, so attach narrowly to the start of that phrase. Native reference maps to LSG 29:2.

Deut.29.2.note: Tests, signs and wonders are separately represented; demonstratives are distributed over the two coordinated French noun phrases. Native reference maps to LSG 29:3.

Deut.29.3.note: Negation scopes the gift of understanding, seeing and hearing. Temporal phrase is fronted; conjunctions absorbed into French list remain contextual. Native reference maps to LSG 29:4.

Deut.30.1.note: Conditional si is supplied by the sequence of Hebrew clauses; returning to heart is idiomatically taking to heart. The destination adverb is implicit in chez lesquelles.

Deut.30.2.note: Return to God and listen to his voice are kept distinct; the whole-heart and whole-soul modifiers are reordered, with possessive suffixes maintained.

Deut.30.3.note: Return captivity is an idiomatic restoration expression rendered ramener tes captifs; the second return verb is rendered encore, and the directional adverb is implicit.

Deut.31.1.note: The verb went is not explicitly translated; encore is an interpretive transition and remains contextual, not a lexical equivalent.

Deut.31.2.note: Age formula son of 120 years is idiomatic; the conjunction in the Hebrew number is omitted in French. Distinguish inability to go out/come in and prohibition of crossing.

Deut.31.3.note: Emphatic pronoun for Joshua is rendered by aussi, a contextual discourse function rather than a lexical pronoun equivalent.

Deut.32.1.note: Imperatives and the two vocatives are distinct; the second conjunction is implicit in parallel poetry.

Deut.32.2.note: The French jussive markers Que are grammatical supports of the two verbs, not lexical translations. Rain, dew and the two comparison groups remain distinct.

Deut.32.3.note: Proclamation of the name and giving greatness/glory are distinct predicates. Possessive suffix of our God is preserved.

Deut.33.1.note: The demonstrative is absorbed in the French presentative voici; blessing, blessing verb and death remain separate.

Deut.33.2.note: The French supplied sending verb belongs to the final fire-of-law clause, not the preceding coming-from-myriads clause. The difficult source expression is retained; no textual emendation.

Deut.33.3.note: Receive is singular in the Hebrew form but plural in French collective rendering. Preserve this number difference; the surrounding pronoun and body-part suffixes remain distinct.

Deut.34.1.note: Native verse explicitly continues into French 34:2 ordinals 1–3. Preserve the land list, causative showing and recipient suffix; do not force the verse boundary.

Deut.34.2.note: The first three French ordinals belong to native verse 1; the remaining regions and western sea are separately mapped. The omitted conjunctions are contextual.

Deut.34.3.note: The Jordan is an interpretive geographic specification in French, not lexically present in the Hebrew plain noun; record as contextual.

Josh.1.1.note: Death of Moses, his status as servant of YHWH, Joshua's father and function are distinct. The speech-introduction formula is absorbed; no additional French lexical word.

Josh.1.2.note: The directional preposition is translated dans, with pour entrer supplied by the French. The recipient suffix in the gift clause is resumed by the children of Israel.

Josh.1.3.note: The place-relative suffix is implicit, and the sole of the foot and its possessive suffix remain separate. The gift verb is perfect in Hebrew but present in French.

Josh.2.1.note: The particularizing phrase is a contextual expansion of the coordination; woman and prostitute form the French single noun, with the indefinite article as support.

Josh.2.2.note: The reporting formula is compressed; the two deictics voici/ici have separate source anchors. The purpose infinitive is explicit.

Josh.2.3.note: The French cleft c'est is a syntactic support for the purpose clause, not a second lexical sense of exploring.

Josh.3.1.note: The resumptive singular pronoun refers to Joshua, and coordination of Joshua and Israel is rendered as accompaniment. Avoid a lexical equivalence between the conjunction and avec.

Josh.3.2.note: The temporal idiom at the end of three days is preserved; the camp's midst is absorbed into parcoururent rather than independently lexicalized.

Josh.3.3.note: Ark, covenant, divine name and priestly carriers are separate anchors. The pronoun referring to the ark is absorbed by the passive participial construction; the following movement is explicit.

Josh.4.1.note: The nation completes the crossing; the discourse formula is contextual. No extra lexical counterpart for the speech-introducing infinitive.

Josh.4.2.note: Repeated man-one distributive formula becomes un homme de chaque tribu. The second occurrence is contextually distributed, not a duplicate lexical occurrence of homme.

Josh.4.3.note: Position of priests' feet and firmness are represented; the relative clause is explicit in French. The original discourse pronouns absorbed by the French imperative and relative construction remain contextual.

Josh.5.1.note: Source divergence: MACULA o060050010282 is suffix Sp3mp, third-person masculine plural, on עבר; LSG says nous. Keep ordinal 39~39 as contextual only and do not claim a person-matched equivalence. Heart melting / absence of spirit are idiomatically rendered as loss of courage / consternation. The Westminster Leningrad Codex reading displayed at https://www.openbible.com/text/joshua/5-1.htm explicitly distinguishes Ketiv עברנו (first-person plural) and Qere עברם (third-person plural). The pinned MACULA projection matches the Qere and LSG matches the Ketiv. This is a documented reading variant, not a source correction.

Josh.5.2.note: Imperative to make knives and the renewed circumcision are distinct. Return/again and second time are both present in the source and retained.

Josh.5.3.note: Araloth is a transliteration of the Hebrew plural foreskins in the place-name expression, not a French semantic translation; retain the link as a name component and document the distinction.

Josh.6.1.note: The second negative existential is rendered by personne plus the negated verb; distinguish the verb's lexical anchor from the negative support.

Josh.6.2.note: The supplied possessive before vaillants soldats refers to Jericho, not to the king. King and military strength remain distinct lexical groups.

Josh.6.3.note: Two circumambulation verbs and the once-per-day pattern are distinct. The supplied French subject and duration preposition are contextual.

Josh.7.1.note: Infidelity and the devoted object are distinct; the second mention of the devoted things is not an independent French equivalent of the full first clause. The genealogy and tribal affiliation are preserved.

Josh.7.2.note: The article on Ai is implicit in French; the direction vers is supplied by the sending construction and attaches to the destination, not lexically to an article.

Josh.7.3.note: The Hebrew movement verb in the proposed troop action is rendered as suffiront; this is a contextual paraphrase of adequacy, not a direct lexical equivalent.

Josh.8.1.note: French contre supplies the target relation; the lexical movement verb is monte. Distinguish the three possessive suffixes and the objects of the gift.

Josh.8.2.note: The two source possessive suffixes are implicit in the definite French articles before spoil and livestock; classify them as contextual rather than lexical.

Josh.8.3.note: The second occurrence of Joshua is replaced by Il. The chosen troop and night-time departure are explicit; the strong-men construction is a single French adjective group.

Josh.9.1.note: The news construction nominalizes hearing; its introductory support is contextual. Correct the article of the sea, not the coast, and distinguish the relative from the supplied copula.

Josh.9.2.note: Together and one mouth are distinct: the second is rendered idiomatically as common agreement. Two opponents are retained separately.

Josh.9.3.note: The temporal connective is supplied by the French subordinate construction; hearing is lexically apprirent.

Josh.10.1.note: Adoni-Tsedek's compound name, capture and devotion of Ai, comparison with Jericho and the Gibeonite peace are preserved despite reordered clauses.

Josh.10.2.note: The source plural they feared is rendered as singular Il eut crainte in French; retain the person/number divergence. The second causal marker is absorbed by the earlier car; the pronoun referring to Gibeon is implicit in the comparative clause.

Josh.10.3.note: The four named kings and their respective cities are retained; the final speech-introduction formula is absorbed into fit dire.

Deut.25.4.note: The prohibition, ox, threshing and its subject suffix are distinct. Grain is an implicit object of threshing, incorporated in the French verbal expression.

Deut.25.5.note: The absence of a son becomes sans laisser de fils; laisser is supplied by the French. The levirate noun and verb are represented by beau-frère and l'épousera comme beau-frère.

Deut.26.4.note: The priest receives the basket from the addressee's hand, then places it before the altar; the object and possessive suffixes have distinct anchors.

Deut.26.5.note: The response verb is expanded as taking the floor; encore is not a separate lexical sense. The Hebrew participle אבד is translated interpretively as nomade; retain the translation's nuance, not a source emendation. The residence and small population are distinct.

Deut.27.4.note: The second dresser is supplied in the French complement of ordonne. It refers to the same erection action, not another Hebrew verb. The plural-to-singular address shift is retained.

Deut.27.5.note: Both occurrences of altar are distinct, as are stone and iron. The French relative and negation are represented without changing the source prohibition.

Deut.28.4.note: The opening blessing is postponed and the summary toutes ces choses is supplied. Both livestock offspring nouns share French portées; the smaller stock possessive belongs to ordinal 23, not the noun.

Deut.28.5.note: The blessing formula covers the basket and kneading trough; the two possessive suffixes remain separate.

Deut.29.4.note: Duration pendant is supplied. The Hebrew plural address in the desert and clothing clauses is rendered as singular in French; preserve this person/number difference. Native verse maps to LSG 29:5.

Deut.29.5.note: Correct forte to the strong-drink noun rather than the purpose conjunction. The drinking subject and negative list supports are contextual. The French copula suis is supplied by the divine self-identification clause. Native verse maps to LSG 29:6.

Deut.30.4.note: Other is an intensifying addition to the extreme edge of heaven, not a second lexical sense. The fetching clause supplies a French subject and motion periphrasis.

Deut.30.5.note: God brings back, gives prosperity and multiplies; ancestral possession and present possession are distinct. Comparative particle corresponds to que.

Deut.31.4.note: These nations is the explicit French antecedent of the Hebrew pronominal indirect object, not a literal noun in the source. Keep Sihon, Og, Amorite kings and land separately anchored.

Deut.31.5.note: Delivery before the addressees becomes delivery to them. The pronoun referring to the nations is distinguished from the audience; commandment is pluralized in French.

Deut.32.4.note: Correct the possessive on work to ses (ordinal 5), not the causal connector Car, which belongs to Hebrew כי. Nominal predications supply French copulas.

Deut.32.5.note: The compressed Hebrew clause has a difficult syntax and the LSG interprets it as blame not attaching to God. The third-person plural blemish suffix is not the possessive ses of God's children; that belongs to unit 6. Keep the former contextually attached and do not manufacture a person-matched equivalence.

Deut.33.4.note: Torah, Moses as giver, communal recipient and inheritance of Jacob's assembly are distinct.

Deut.33.5.note: Jeshurun is rendered Israël, a referential equivalence rather than transliteration. The gathered heads and tribes are distinguished; the French does not explicitly identify the king beyond the pronoun.

Deut.34.4.note: The repeated promise of giving and the showing of the land are separate clauses. French de donner in the first clause is contextual, while the actual gift verb is in the quotation. The destination adverb and negated crossing are distinct.

Deut.34.5.note: Death of Moses, location and servant designation are separately anchored. The idiom according to the mouth of YHWH is rendered according to the order of YHWH.

Josh.1.4.note: The territorial boundaries are rearranged around the French possessive construction. The two river references, the Euphrates, Hittite land and western sea are retained. The demonstrative on Lebanon is implicit.

Josh.1.5.note: The promise has two distinct negative verbs; French subject pronouns before each are grammatical supports. The duration idiom is compressed as tant que tu vivras.

Josh.2.4.note: The deictic affirmation becomes il est vrai que; the plural pronoun in the origin question is lexical ils, but the copula is supplied.

Josh.2.5.note: The causal/assuring conjunction is represented as et in French; it is a contextual discourse relation rather than a direct lexical equivalent. The men are resumed by a pronoun.

Josh.3.4.note: The source purpose that you may know is recast as the ark showing the way. This is a contextual paraphrase, not a direct lexical match for ידע. The past-time idiom is rendered encore.

Josh.3.5.note: The command to sanctify oneself, tomorrow, YHWH's action and wonders in the people's midst remain distinct.

Josh.4.4.note: The second man-one occurrence is the distributive repetition rendered chaque; do not make a duplicate lexical occurrence of homme.

Josh.4.5.note: Joshua is replaced by the French pronoun Il; the second-person plural dative is absorbed into de vous in the distributive imperative, not the lifting verb itself.

Josh.5.4.note: The object pronoun is supplied with circumcision. The temporal preposition at the time of departure is rendered après in French, a contextual temporal interpretation.

Josh.5.5.note: Egypt is an explicit addition to the first departure participle, based on the previous verse; the later Egypt is explicit. The possessive suffix in their departure is implicit in the French article.

Josh.6.4.note: The ram-horn designation יובל is interpreted in LSG as retentissantes; it describes the instruments but is not a direct lexical equivalent of resonant. The repeated seven counts and seventh day remain distinct.

Josh.6.5.note: The ram-horn designation has the same interpretive rendering as in verse 4. The wall falling beneath itself is rendered as collapse, with the local suffix contextually absorbed.

Josh.7.4.note: The approximate troop count and flight are distinct. The source partitive from the people and destination adverb are implicit in the French movement clause.

Josh.7.5.note: The source heart melts and becomes water is rendered by loss of courage and consternation. Keep the lexical metaphor's heart/courage anchor and classify the water imagery as contextual rather than a French lexical occurrence.

Josh.8.4.note: The attention marker literally uses see but the LSG says Écoutez. Classify it as a contextual discourse function, not an ordinary sense of the visual verb. The duplicated city reference is implicit in the ambush instruction.

Josh.8.5.note: The French relative copula is supplied; approach and retreat are distinct. The first-time comparison remains separate from the conditional sortie.

Josh.9.4.note: The provisions rendering of the difficult preparation verb is retained as a translation decision; old sacks and old torn and mended wineskins are distinct. No external textual emendation is introduced.

Josh.9.5.note: The possessive suffix on their provisions becomes a French relative clause with an added avoir; it is a contextual expansion. Dryness and crumbling of bread are distinct.

Josh.10.4.note: The Hebrew connective introduces the result/purpose of the requested aid; French afin que is contextual rather than a direct lexical equivalent of waw. The peace agreement has distinct participants.

Josh.10.5.note: The explicit pronoun they refers to the five kings and is resumed by ils in the camping clause. The French motion auxiliary is supplied; coordination with their armies is contextual accompaniment, not a direct lexical equivalence.

Deut.28.69.note: The native chapter boundary differs from LSG. Both occurrences of covenant-making are distinct; Moab and Horeb remain distinct anchors. The initial demonstrative is absorbed into the presentative voici and is classified as contextual.

Deut.25.10.note: Name of the house is recast as house; name is not a lexical occurrence of maison. Shoe-removal epithet is a grouped correspondence.

Deut.27.6.note: Whole/undamaged stones rendered brutes; preserve LSG interpretation.

Deut.28.7.note: Defeat of enemies is recast as giving victory: grouped semantic correspondence.

Deut.28.9.note: Causative establishing is recast as a state; divine agency is implicit in this clause.

Deut.29.11.note: The repeated covenant expression is a French expansion of the oath clause; no additional Hebrew covenant noun.

Deut.31.7.note: The feminine object suffix refers to the land (en); the plural object pronoun refers to the people (les).

Deut.31.11.note: The source idiom 'in their ears' is rendered en leur présence, contextual.

Deut.32.6.note: LSG interprets repayment to YHWH as holding him responsible; preserve the translation, without changing Hebrew.

Deut.32.12.note: French son peuple explicates the pronominal reference to Jacob/Israel.

Deut.33.6.note: The difficult numerical expression is rendered nombreux in LSG; retain this translation, not a textual correction.

Deut.34.6.note: LSG explicitly names YHWH as the burial agent; the source has only a third-person singular verb.

Deut.34.11.note: The source divine name is rendered Dieu here; retain the referential link.

Josh.2.8.note: Explicit referents les espions and Rahab are supplied in French in place of Hebrew pronouns.

Josh.2.11.note: Negated rising of spirit rendered as abattus; retain the semantic negation as a grouped paraphrase.

Josh.2.12.note: Preserve explicit cross-verse links to the opening of LSG 2:13.

Josh.4.6.note: Tomorrow is rendered un jour generically in LSG.

Josh.5.12.note: Passover is explicit only in French here; already attached contextually to lendemain.

Josh.6.6.note: Yobel is the horn designation, interpretively retentissantes in LSG; contextual classification applied consistently through verses 8 and 13.

Josh.7.7.note: The wish to have been willing to remain is rendered as wishing to have known to remain; do not treat savoir as a direct lexical sense.

Josh.8.11.note: The valley between the armies and Ai becomes a French separation clause; place name resumed by dont.

Josh.9.7.note: Singular Hebrew addressee and plural French address are preserved.

Deut.25.19.note: The French delivery clause is an expansion of the rest-from-enemies idiom; retain contextual links, not a new Hebrew verb.

Deut.26.17.note: The declaration formula is interpreted as making a promise, preserved without changing the source.

Deut.29.18.note: The difficult saturated/thirsty metaphor is rendered ivresse/soif in LSG.

Deut.29.21.note: Native אמר (will say) is not independently expressed in LSG 29:22. Its discourse is completed by shared diront in LSG 29:24 ordinal 4, verified against the pinned LSG chapter. Contextual cross-verse link; the lexical occurrence belongs to native 29:23.

Deut.30.20.note: The Hebrew pronoun in 'he is your life' is rendered as the antecedent cela and a supplied dependency verb in LSG.

Deut.32.17.note: Hebrew šēdîm (demons) is rendered idoles in LSG; retain the translation-specific link, not an asserted general dictionary sense.

Deut.32.21.note: Corrected swapped negative/divine-noun and nation/adjective/verb anchors; preserve both parallel clauses.

Deut.33.15.note: The mountain imagery is interpreted as produce in the French.

Deut.33.21.note: Seeing/selecting and the leaders of the people are rendered interpretively; preserve LSG without source emendation.

Josh.2.14.note: The life-for-life pledge is recast as readiness to die; the supplied readiness phrase is contextual.

Josh.3.16.note: The French completeness adverb corresponds to the completion verb, distinct from the passive auxiliary of being cut off.

Josh.5.14.note: Corrected shifted chief/army/YHWH/now anchors, retaining the supplied copula as contextual.

Josh.6.20.note: French supplies priests as trumpet-blowers; first occurrence of people is resumed by il.

Josh.7.17.note: Native men vs LSG houses; contextual correspondence, not lexical equivalence.

Josh.8.16.note: Ai is rendered by ville here.

Josh.9.14.note: Mouth of YHWH rendered as consulting YHWH; contextual link.

Josh.9.15.note: Treaty beneficiaries and oath beneficiaries distinguished.

Deut.27.26.note: LSG supplies a second negative and relative construction; these are contextual rather than a second native negation.

Deut.28.22.note: Disease names retain the LSG interpretive equivalents; no medical or lexical modernization.

Deut.28.30.note: French obscures the conjunction before the vineyard clause; anchor the contextual relation to that clause.

Deut.28.34.note: French causative construction for the native state of becoming mad.

Deut.29.22.note: Preserve explicit cross-verse links to LSG 29:22 for the sulfur and salt phrase.

Deut.29.25.note: YHWH is explicit in the LSG but the native subject is implicit.

Deut.28.49.note: French relative construction expresses native comparison; retain eagle simile.

Deut.31.23.note: LSG supplies YHWH as the speaker; native subject is implicit.

Deut.31.29.note: Temporal idiom 'in the latter days' rendered by finira par; contextual alignment.

Deut.33.24.note: LSG specifies Israel where native reads sons; contextual explicit referent.

Deut.33.26.note: Jeshurun rendered by Israel; referential correspondence, not an identical name.

Deut.33.27.note: Second French refuge expression is supplied; contextual link.

Deut.28.55.note: Native preposition withholding is rendered as French negation; contextual.

Deut.28.57.note: French supplies withholding clause from the preceding context.

Deut.28.65.note: Noun phrases supply possessives in French; narrow contextual anchors instead of a whole clause.

Deut.32.25.note: French supplies impersonal subject and comparison construction.

Deut.32.35.note: French negated delay expresses native haste.

Deut.32.39.note: Native emphatic pronoun hu is rendered Dieu explicitly; context rather than lexical equivalent. French reverses the order of killing and giving life; existing map preserves the correct verbs.

Deut.32.43.note: LSG supplies the divine name as subject. Preserve the native textual scope without adding material from other witnesses.

Deut.32.44.note: Native Hoshea, LSG Josué, referentially same person; retain each source name.

Deut.32.46.note: French infinitival command structure recasts native relative clause.

Josh.2.23.note: Jordan supplied explicitly in French; contextual destination of crossing.

Josh.6.26.note: French temporal cleft expresses native time phrase.

Josh.7.22.note: Acan is explicit in the LSG; native possessive suffix only.

Josh.8.22.note: French passive enveloppés summarizes native position between two groups.

Josh.8.26.note: Ai is implicit in French; native name retained contextually.

Josh.8.29.note: LSG supplies leaving the body hanging; contextual relation to hanging verb.

Josh.8.32.note: Joshua explicit in French, implicit subject in native.

Josh.9.26.note: LSG expands native 'thus' to prior decision.

Josh.9.27.note: Native Joshua rendered by French pronoun; divine name later supplied contextually.

Josh.10.27.note: LSG relative clause about stones remaining paraphrases the temporal expression.

Josh.10.28.note: Native feminine object pronoun rendered as la ville.

Josh.10.35.note: Joshua explicit in French in the second clause, native subject implicit.

Josh.10.37.note: Possessive suffix rendered as a relative clause; Joshua supplied in French as subject.

Josh.10.39.note: Native 'thus' attaches to the action of treating Debir, not to the supplied proper name Joshua.

Josh.10.40.note: French repeats the initial defeat verb for the kings.

Josh.4.2.note: Hebrew distributive repetition of one man, one man is rendered un homme de chaque [tribu]. Use the smallest complete repeated expression as a single many-to-many translation correspondence, not a second literal man or number.

Josh.4.4.note: Same distributive construction and French rendering as 4:2; apply consistently.

Deut.25.5.note: The Hebrew noun-plus-adjective expression איש זר is rendered un étranger, a substantivized adjective; group both native lexical components without inventing a second French noun.

Josh.10.39.note: The comparative particle כן resumes the preceding comparison; Joshua is an explicit French subject supplied for the implicit subject of עשה. Attach each to the appropriate expression rather than treating the comparative as a personal name.
